}}'''''Sarracenia purpurea''''', the '''purple pitcher plant''', '''northern pitcher plant''', '''turtle socks''', or '''side-saddle flower''', is a [[carnivorous plant]] in the family [[Sarraceniaceae]].

==Taxonomy==
The species is further divided into two [[subspecies]], ''S. purpurea'' subsp. ''purpurea'' and ''S. purpurea'' subsp. ''venosa''. The former is found north of [[New Jersey]] north, while the latter is found south of [[New Jersey]] and tolerates warmer temperatures.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

==Carnivory==
[[File:Sarracenia purpurea 009.jpg|thumb|''S. purpurea'' with springtails, ''[[Saint-Narcisse|St-Narcisse]], [[Quebec]], [[Canada]]''|left]][[File:Lebia grandis.jpg|thumb|''[[Lebia grandis]]'' ground beetle trapped inside pitcher]]Like other species of ''[[Sarracenia]]'', ''S. purpurea'' obtains most of its nutrients through prey capture.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Wakefield AE |author2=Gotelli NJ |author3=Wittman SE |author4=Ellison AM | title=Prey addition alters nutrient stoichiometry of the carnivorous plant ''Sarracenia purpurea'' | journal=Ecology | volume=86 | year=2005 | pages=1737–1743 | url=http://www.esajournals.org/esaonline/?request=get-abstract&issn=0012-9658&volume=086&issue=07&page=1737 | doi=10.1890/04-1673 | type=abstract | issue=7|bibcode=2005Ecol...86.1737W | url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, prey acquisition is said to be inefficient, with less than 1% of the visiting prey captured within the pitcher.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Newell SJ |author2=Nastase AJ | title=Efficiency of nutrient capture by ''Sarracenia purpurea'' (Sarraceniaceae), the Northern Pitcher Plant | journal=American Journal of Botany | volume=85 | year=1998 | pages=88–91 | doi=10.2307/2446558 | issue=1 | jstor=2446558|s2cid=16021826 }}</ref> Even so, anecdotal evidence by growers often shows that pitchers quickly fill up with prey during the warm summer months. Prey fall into the pitcher and drown in the rainwater that collects in the base of each leaf.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

Prey items, such as [[Diptera|flies]], [[ant]]s, [[spider]]s, and even [[moth]]s or [[hornets]], are then digested by an invertebrate community, made up mostly by the mosquito ''[[Wyeomyia smithii]]'' and the midge ''[[Metriocnemus knabi]]''.{{citation needed|date=December 2021}} The relationship between ''W. smithii'' and ''S. purpurea'' is an example of [[commensalism]].<ref>C. Michael Hogan. 2011. [http://editors.eol.org/eoearth/wiki/Commensalism ''Commensalism''. Topic Ed. M.Mcginley. Ed-in-chief C.J.Cleveland. Encyclopedia of Earth. National Council for Science and the Environment. Washington DC]</ref>

[[Protist]]s, [[rotifer]]s (including ''[[Habrotrocha rosa]]''), and bacteria form the base of [[inquiline]] [[food web]] that shreds and mineralizes available prey, making nutrients available to the plant.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Heard SB | title=Pitcher plant midges and mosquitoes: a processing chain commensalism | journal=Ecology | volume=75 | year=1994 | pages=1647–1660 | doi=10.2307/1939625 | type=abstract | issue=6 | jstor=1939625| bibcode=1994Ecol...75.1647H }}</ref><ref name="Mouquet 2008">{{cite journal |author1=Mouquet N. |author2=Daufresne T. |author3=Gray S. M. |author4=Miller T. E. | year = 2008 | title = Modelling the relationship between a pitcher plant (''Sarracenia purpurea'') and its phytotelma community: mutualism or parasitism? | journal = Functional Ecology | volume = 22 | issue = 4| pages = 728–737 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2435.2008.01421.x | doi-access = free |bibcode=2008FuEco..22..728M }}</ref><ref name="Peterson 2008">{{cite journal |author1=Peterson C. N. |author2=Day S. |author3=Wolfe B. E. |author4=Ellison A. M. |author5=Kolter R. |author6=Pringle A. | year = 2008 | title = A keystone predator controls bacterial diversity in the pitcher-plant (''Sarracenia purpurea'') microecosystem | journal = Environmental Microbiology | volume = 10 | issue = 9| pages = 2257–2266 | doi = 10.1111/j.1462-2920.2008.01648.x | pmid = 18479443 |bibcode=2008EnvMi..10.2257P }}</ref> New pitcher leaves do produce [[digestive enzyme]]s such as [[hydrolase]]s and [[protease]]s, but as the individual leaves get older into their second year, digestion of prey material is aided by the community of bacteria that live within the pitchers.<ref name="Rice 2007">Rice, Barry. (2007). [http://www.sarracenia.com/faq/faq5538.html About ''Sarracenia purpurea'', the purple pitcher plant]. The Carnivorous Plant FAQ. Accessed online: 21 June 2008.</ref><ref name="Gallie and Chang 1997">{{cite journal |author1=Gallie D. Regulation of secretory hydrolase expression during development and in response to resources | doi-access=free | journal = Plant Physiology | volume = 115 | issue = 4| pages = 1461–1471 | pmid = 9414556 | doi = 10.1104/pp.115.4.1461 | pmc = 158611 }}</ref>

=== Vertebrate prey ===
[[File:Sarracenia purpurea ssp. purpurea and Eastern newt, Vermont, US imported from iNaturalist photo 448318281.jpg|thumb|''S. p. purpurea'' with a trapped [[eastern newt]], in Vermont.]]''S. purpurea'' traps juvenile [[eastern newt]]s with enough regularity that nearly 20% of plants in an [[Ontario]] population were found to contain one or more salamanders in a 2019 study. The salamanders were observed to die within three to nineteen days, and may be killed as the small pools of water in the plant are heated by the sun. A single salamander could provide hundreds to thousands of times the nutrients of invertebrate prey, but it is not known how efficiently ''S. purpurea'' is able to digest them.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/2019/06/salamanders-bogs-carnivorous-plants/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190613054320/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/2019/06/salamanders-bogs-carnivorous-plants/|archive-date=June 13, 2019|title=Carnivorous plants eat far more salamanders than scientists thought|first=Sandrine|last=Ceurstemont|publisher=National Geographic|year=2019|access-date=31 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Moldowan |first1=Patrick D. |last2=Smith |first2=M. Alex |last3=Baldwin |first3=Teskey |last4=Bartley |first4=Timothy |last5=Rollinson |first5=Njal |last6=Wynen |first6=Hannah |date=2019 |title=Nature's pitfall trap: salamanders as rich prey for carnivorous plants in a nutrient-poor northern bog ecosystem |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecy.2770 |journal=Ecology |language=en |volume=100 |issue=10 |pages=e02770 |doi=10.1002/ecy.2770 |pmid=31165468 |bibcode=2019Ecol..100E2770M |issn=1939-9170|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This behaviour has also been recorded occurring in [[Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Butler |first1=Jessica L. |last2=Atwater |first2=Daniel Z. |last3=Ellison |first3=Aaron M. |date=March 2005 |title=Red-spotted Newts: An Unusual Nutrient Source for Northern Pitcher Plants |url=http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.1656/1092-6194%282005%29012%5B0001%3ARNAUNS%5D2.0.CO%3B2 |journal=Northeastern Naturalist |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1656/1092-6194(2005)012[0001:RNAUNS]2.0.CO;2 |issn=1092-6194|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Distribution==
Species of ''Sarracenia'' grow in nutrient-poor, acid bogs.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2009.01014.x | title=Murderous plants: Victorian Gothic, Darwin and modern insights into vegetable carnivory | year=2009 | last1=Chase | first1=Mark W. | last2=Christenhusz | first2=Maarten J. M. | last3=Sanders | first3=Dawn | last4=Fay | first4=Michael F. | journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society | volume=161 | issue=4 | pages=329–356 | doi-access=free }}</ref> ''S. purpurea''<nowiki/>'s range includes the [[East coast of the United States|Eastern seaboard]], the [[Great Lakes region]], all of [[Canada]] (except Nunavut and Yukon), Washington state, and [[Alaska]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/plant-profile/SAPU4|title=USDA Distribution map of ''Sarracenia purpurea''|work=USDA Plants Database}}</ref> That makes it the most common and broadly distributed [[pitcher plant]], as well as the only member of the genus that inhabits [[temperate|cold temperate]] [[climates]]. How the species traveled so far is still a mystery. From what is known so far the Sarracenia has a median seed dispersal distance of 5 cm (2 inches), which is not far enough to explain the plant's widespread occurrence throughout North America.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.3732/ajb.89.6.1024 | title=Seed dispersal and seedling establishment of Sarracenia purpurea (Sarraceniaceae) | year=2002 | last1=Ellison | first1=A. M. | last2=Parker | first2=J. N. | journal=American Journal of Botany | volume=89 | issue=6 | pages=1024–1026 | pmid=21665703 }}</ref> It is endangered or vulnerable over much of the southern part of its range.<ref name=NS/> Most varieties along the [[Gulf Coast of the United States]] that were once identified as ''Sarracenia purpurea'' have since been reclassified as ''[[Sarracenia rosea]]''.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

It is an [[introduced species|introduced]] and [[naturalized species]] in Europe and the northwestern US.<ref name="EPPO-alert">{{cite web | title=''Sarracenia purpurea'' | website=EPPO ([[European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization]]) | url=http://www.eppo.int/ACTIVITIES/plant_quarantine/alert_list_plants/sarracenia_purpurea | access-date=2021-07-08 | archive-date=2023-03-23 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230323175819/https://eppo.int/ACTIVITIES/plant_quarantine/alert_list_plants/sarracenia_purpurea }}</ref> It is found in habitats of the native carnivorous species ''[[Darlingtonia californica]]'', in the [[Klamath Mountains]] and northern [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]].<ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=43271 Jepson Manual eFlora (TJM2) treatment of ''Sarracenia purpurea''] − naturalized distribution in California</ref> The plant has also been recorded in [[Washington state]], [[Austria]], the [[Czech Republic]], [[Denmark]], [[France]], [[Germany]], [[Ireland]], [[Sweden]], [[Switzerland]], and the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name="EPPO-alert" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Sarracenia purpurea L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30030166-2 |website=Kewscience. Plants of the World online |access-date=14 January 2021}}</ref> In Britain and Ireland purple pitcher plant have been introduced into some heather-rich [[Bog|peatbogs]] and with the mild climate have integrated into the local flora of some specific areas. But observations made by researchers throughout almost a century have seen no signs of the plant spreading to other bogs, because of the highly fragmented distribution of bogs in Britain and Ireland.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Agyepong-Parsons |first1=James |title=Suck Stick Drip |journal=BBC Wildlife |date=January 2021 |pages=32–5}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Foss, P.J.  |author2=O'Connell, C.A.  |name-list-style=amp | year = 1985 | title = Notes on the ecology of ''Sarracenia purpurea'' L. on Irish peatlands | journal = The Irish Naturalists' Journal | volume = 21 | issue = 10 | pages = 440–443| jstor = 25538921 }}</ref>

==Uses==
=== Symbolic ===
The species is the floral emblem of the [[Canada|Canadian]] province of [[Newfoundland and Labrador]] since 1954. [[Queen Victoria]] was the first to select the plant as a provincial symbol to be portrayed on the province's penny until 1938.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Heritage |first=Canadian |date=2017-08-15 |title=Newfoundland and Labrador |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/provincial-territorial-symbols-canada/newfoundland-and-labrador.html |access-date=2024-06-16 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref>

===Ornamental===
''Sarracenia purpurea'' is cultivated as an ornamental plant. It is fairly [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]], but requires a reliably damp soil in a sheltered position, with full or partial sunlight. The [[subspecies]] ''S. purpurea'' ssp. ''purpurea'' has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/96343/Sarracenia-purpurea-subsp-purpurea/Details | title = ''Sarracenia purpurea'' subsp. ''purpurea'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>

=== Medicinal ===
It was used as a [[medicinal plant]] by [[Native Americans of the United States|Native American]] and [[First Nations in Canada|First Nation]] tribes in its northeastern and Great Lakes distribution ranges, including the [[Algonquin people|Algonquin]], [[Cree]], [[Iroquois]], and [[Mi'kmaq|Mi'kmaq (Micmac)]] peoples,<!-- <ref>[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Sarracenia+purpurea University of Michigan - Dearborn: Native American Ethnobotanyof ''Sarracenia purpurea'']</ref> --><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/species/3588/| title=Sarracenia purpurea L. Documented uses |work= Native American Ethnobotany Database }}</ref> primarily for use in treating [[smallpox]] by means of a root infusion.<ref>{{cite book |title= American Medicinal Plants: An Illustrated and Descriptive Guide to Plants Indigenous to and Naturalized in the United States which are Used in Medicine |author= Charles Frederick Millspaugh |edition= illustrated |publisher= Courier Corporation |year= 1892 |isbn= 978-0-486-23034-4 |page= [https://archive.org/details/americanmedicina00mill_0/page/76 76] |url-access= registration |url= https://archive.org/details/americanmedicina00mill_0/page/76 }}</ref> A 2012 study suggests ''Sarracenia purpurea'' is effective as a treatment for viruses in the [[Orthopoxvirus]] family, including the smallpox virus, through inhibition of early virus transcription.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Arndt|first1=William|last2=Mitnik|first2=Chandra|last3=Denzler|first3=Karen L.|last4=White|first4=Stacy|last5=Waters|first5=Robert|last6=Jacobs|first6=Bertram L.|last7=Rochon|first7=Yvan|last8=Olson|first8=Victoria A.|last9=Damon|first9=Inger K.|last10=Langland|first10=Jeffrey O.|date=2012-03-09|title=In Vitro Characterization of a Nineteenth-Century Therapy for Smallpox|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=7|issue=3|article-number=e32610|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0032610|issn=1932-6203|pmc=3302891|pmid=22427855|bibcode=2012PLoSO...732610A|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Biocontrol===
''Sarracenia purpurea'' pitchers have been investigated as a biocontrol for the Asian Hornet ''[[Vespa velutina]]'' in Europe,<ref>{{cite bioRxiv |title=Variation in colour signals among Sarracenia pitcher plants and the potential role of areoles in the attraction of flying Hymenoptera |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.09.15.460199 |year=2021 |last1=Dupont |first1=Corentin |last2=Villemant |first2=Claire |last3=Hatterman |first3=Tom |last4=Pratviel |first4=Jeremie |last5=Gaume |first5=Laurence |last6=Gomez |first6=Doris }}</ref> as they act as natural bottle traps in which hornets have been observed to be trapped. The hybrids used in the study, S. x "Juthatip Soper" and S. x "Evendine", were deemed too unselective, but the researchers proposed that trying other pitcher plant species may be more effective.<ref name="failed-biocontrol">{{ Cite journal | title=Wycke M-A, Perrocheau R, Darrouzet E (2018) Sarracenia carnivorous plants cannot serve as efficient biological control of the invasive hornet Vespa velutina nigrithorax in Europe. Rethinking Ecology 3: 41-50. DOI 10.3897/rethinkingecology.3.28516 | journal=Rethinking Ecology | date=11 December 2018 | volume=3 | pages=41–50 | doi=10.3897/rethinkingecology.3.28516 | s2cid=91375714 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Salt-not-yet">{{ cite web | url=http://www.botany.one/2018/11/can-carnivorous-plants-control-an-invasive-hornet/ | title=Can carnivorous plants control an invasive hornet? | date=20 November 2018 }}</ref>
